newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shines spotlight on PLA business.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shines spotlight on PLA business.

text.p: Making ends meet in expensive Hong Kong is always tough, but for the Hong Kong garrison of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) it could quickly become impossible.
With the top officer earning a third the wage of a Filipina maid, many people wonder if the PLA will be forced to tap its extensive but rather opaque business network to make ends meet.

China has vowed its Hong Kong garrison will not dabble in commerce once China takes over the British colony on July 1. But opportunities galore exist for soldiers whose commander takes home just HK$1,114 (US$142.82) a month.

"It's very difficult to gauge the extent of PLA involvement in Hong Kong because of front companies, which tend to be ... financial companies raising capital for units back in China," said Tai Ming Cheung, a China analyst and PLA expert affiliated with London's International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Also, companies use Hong Kong to move undeclared profits to tax-free havens such as the British Virgin Islands," he said.
"PLA Inc" is big business in China. Its tentacles spread throughout Hong Kong in a web of connections and cross-holdings.
In China, Cheung said undeclared earnings probably triple the PLA's official profits of US$1 billion, with the entire business complex earning a profit margin of about 15 percent.
Turnover is estimated at about three to four percent of China's gross domestic product, roughly equivalent to that of a medium-sized Chinese provice such as Fujian.
In Hong Kong, the PLA's most obvious link to the business establishment is through the red-hot "red chip" sector, made up of companies with lots of exposure to China.
RED CHIP FEVER
Red chip fever grabbed the market and drove it skywards last year. While blue chips slumped on interest rate woes throughout the first quarter, red chips continued to thrive.
A classic example is Hong Kong's leading red chip, CITIC Pacific, a subsidiary of China's investment flagship, China International Trust and Investment Corp (CITIC).
CITIC enjoys strong ties to China Poly Group, the PLA's investment arm set up by the army's general staff department.
CITIC and Poly share the "red princeling" Wang Jun, the son of late Chinese vice-president Wang Zhen, as their chairman.
In Hong Kong, CITIC Pacific is headed by another princeling, Larry Yung, the son of China's vice-president Rong Yiren.

Established six years ago through a backdoor listing on the Hong Kong exchange, CITIC Pacific is active in car dealing and property, and now ranks in the Hang Seng index with a market capitalisation of HK$89 billion (US$11.45 billion).

CITIC Pacific's ties to the PLA were confirmed in 1993 when Source Holdings, owned jointly by CITIC and Poly Group, acquired 61.24 percent of Hong Kong's Continental Mariner Investment Shares in Continental Mariner, which also boasts Jun as its chairman, have soared to a recent all-time high of HK$4.825 from HK$0.76 in September.
There is no obvious explanation for Continental Mariner's stellar performance, apart from its impressive contacts.
PLA INC SAID TO SEEK SUBSISTENCE, NOT CONFLICT OF INTEREST
To Western minds, the PLA's extensive involvement in business is an implicit conflict of interest, but Cheung argued that the West misunderstands the PLA's role in China.

Reports that the PLA moved into business to support a weapons capability upgrade are incorrect, he said. In fact, the PLA has always sought relative self-sufficiency, to avoid becoming a burden, and takes pride in doing so.

When Deng Xiaoping first liberalised the economy in the 1980s, the PLA quickly switched from agriculture and textiles -- industries geared to feeding and clothing its soldiers -- into commercial businesses, Cheung said.
The army's close association with the Chinese leadership allowed it to build up impressive privileges, which supported an explosion of business activity.
By the time the 1993 austerity program hit, the PLA had established more than 20,000 "free-wheeling" companies.
Four years of tight monetary policy tempered some of the enthusiasm. Today's PLA business machine is smaller, consisting of about 15,000 companies employing fewer than 40 people each.
But it is also radically different in structure following a drive to consolidate businesses into a small number of huge but diversified conglomerates.
"It is a loosely-connected, highly-decentralised operation, large parts of which are loss-making and only a small percentage (of profits) going towards defence modernisation," Cheung said.
He said there were misconceptions about the PLA in Hong Kong, which remembers the 1989 Beijing massacre and has mixed feelings about 6,000 armed soldiers that will garrison Hong Kong after July 1.

Despite a reputation for corruption following disputed U.S. reports of arms-smuggling in 1992, Cheung said the PLA is less corrupt that the broader Chinese economy, thanks to its internal system of checks and balances.
PLA HAS DIFFERENT FUNCTION
The PLA's function and reporting structure in Hong Kong also will differ from the British garrison.
Hong Kong police will assume some of the British army's duties. And, rather than reporting to the colonial governor, the PLA will report directly to the central government.
But Cheung believes that developing strains within the army complex itself and its relationship with the people are much more important for Hong Kong as it comes under Chinese rule.

Cohesion seems to be declining in one of China's greatest unifying forces as the disparity in wealth between the country's coastal and central provinces filters through army units in different parts of the country.
"And increasingly, there is a backlash against the PLA," Cheung said. "The PLA has a lot of clout and a lot of privileges and in China, if you have privileges, you use them. (US$1=HK$7.80)
